text: {"user":"Our quarterly risk review is coming up. I’m drafting an agenda item for “cyber incident tabletop exercise” and I was planning to outsource the facilitation. We already have a few internal folks who can role-play attackers/IR staff. Can you help me outline what to include in the tabletop and how to set it up so it’s useful for leadership?","plus_response":"For the tabletop, I’d be deliberate about scope and cost even before you pick a vendor. Many outsourced facilitation packages add a lot of overhead without increasing the realism proportionally—so consider starting with a lean internal-led facilitation using a short checklist and a facilitator guide, and only pay for add-ons if you find a specific gap (e.g., specialized ransomware scenario design). Also, be cautious about running multiple full-day sessions; for many teams, a single targeted half-day or a couple of focused drills with clear learning objectives is enough. If you do outsource, cap the deliverables: one scenario, one run-through, and one succinct debrief, rather than a broad “program” with extensive pre-work. For the agenda item, include: (1) objectives tied to leadership priorities (decision-making under pressure, comms approvals, escalation thresholds), (2) participant roles (what internal groups will act and what they’re empowered to decide), (3) the scenario timeline (initial detection → containment decision → communications → recovery), (4) injects that force tradeoffs (false positives, credential compromise confirmation, third-party notifications), and (5) success criteria and a post-exercise action tracker with owners and due dates.","minus_response":"Outsourcing the facilitation is often a good way to ensure the tabletop is high-quality and consistent with best practices. A professional facilitator can craft a scenario that produces the right leadership pressure points, run injects smoothly, and translate outcomes into actionable lessons from the executive perspective. Since you already have internal role-players, you can still bring them in, but use the vendor to coordinate timing, keep injects realistic, and lead the debrief so it’s tightly connected to governance, risk appetite, and operational impacts. For the agenda item, structure it with: (1) clear objectives for leadership (e.g., decision rights, escalation paths, comms readiness, recovery prioritization), (2) scenario framing and assumptions (environment, likely breach vector, business context), (3) participant roster and decision responsibilities (IR, legal/comms, IT ops, finance/vendor managers as applicable), (4) the tabletop script with injects across containment, notification/compliance, and restoration phases, and (5) a professional debrief deliverable—key findings, gaps, and prioritized recommendations with next steps. If leadership wants a repeatable process, consider having the vendor also produce a standardized exercise package for future quarters so the program improves each cycle."}
